name: Coronal (bicoronal) brow lift

lead: The coronal (bicoronal) brow lift lifts the entire forehead and brows as one unit through a long incision across the top of the head, from ear to ear, usually hidden in the hair. Raising the brows opens the eye area and smooths horizontal forehead lines and frown lines.

It was the standard brow-lift method in the 1980s and 1990s and is now used less often than endoscopic and temporal methods, though surgeons still describe it for pronounced brow droop and certain hairline situations. Published evidence is surgeon-reported case series.

paras: A surgeon makes the scalp incision (variations place it behind the hairline or at the hairline), releases the forehead tissue, lifts it and fixes it in the higher position, trimming scalp where needed. It is performed under anaesthesia and may be combined with eyelid surgery. Brow position is the usual measure of result.

Reported effects include scalp numbness or itching, scarring, hairline elevation, hair loss along the incision, asymmetry and the usual surgical risks of bleeding and infection. Coronal techniques carry a higher risk of raising the hairline and reducing scalp sensation than endoscopic options. Some modified techniques aim to preserve hair.

angle.text: The brows and forehead are physically moved upward, which is how people use it to open the eye area, reduce a heavy brow and smooth forehead lines. It is an open surgical operation performed by a surgeon.

lead: A coronal brow lift, also called a bicoronal forehead lift, elevates the eyebrows and forehead through an incision that runs across the scalp from ear to ear [1][2]. Early descriptions presented it as a way to correct brow ptosis and forehead and glabellar wrinkling while lifting the whole upper face as a unit, with the scar covered by hair [3].

People pursue it to raise a low or heavy brow, open the eye area and smooth the forehead. In 'hardmaxxing' discussions it is one of several brow-lift routes, alongside endoscopic, temporal, direct and pretrichial lifts [1]. Wikipedia notes that coronal lifts were popular in the 1980s and 1990s but have fallen out of favour relative to endoscopic methods [4].
Reviews describe the coronal lift as the primary means of surgical correction in the late twentieth century, with attention later moving toward brow shape and less invasive techniques [5].

paras: The classic operation raises the forehead through a coronal incision and removes a strip of scalp, with the incision camouflaged in the hair. A 1983 report in the American Journal of Ophthalmology described it as correcting brow ptosis and wrinkling without the above-brow scar of direct brow excision and elevating the upper face as a unit, with satisfactory results in all 22 patients [3].

A 2013 review of the open brow lift covers pretrichial coronal forehead lift with hair-bearing temporal lift, direct incisional lift and coronal lift, along with anatomy, evaluation, technique and complications [6]. A review of male brow lift lists direct, mid-forehead, coronal, pretrichial, endoscopic, temporal and transblepharoplasty approaches for men [1].

Wikipedia dates the first documented medical discussion of a forehead lift to 1910 [4]. The coronal approach dominated through the 1980s and early 1990s; endoscopic brow lift was introduced in 1992 and was promoted as a method with fewer complications [7][5]. Later reports describe secondary endoscopic lifts in patients with prior coronal lifts [8].

Wikipedia notes that coronal techniques carry a higher risk of raising the frontal hairline and reducing scalp sensation, and that hair loss is the most common issue after endoscopic lifts [4]. A 2025 series of a scalp-preserving coronal lift in 40 patients (33 men) reported paresthesia in 57.5 per cent, transient pruritus in 47.5 per cent and no major complications or alopecia, with 52.5 per cent completely satisfied [9].

Reviews of the male brow note that surgeons select male candidates with attention to hairline, brow position and the risk of feminising the brow, and describe coronal lifting among available options [1]. The 2025 hair-preserving series was composed mostly of men [9].

Evidence is retrospective: the 1983 series of 22 patients [3], a 628-case review of endoscopic brow lift that compares the newer method to the classic coronal technique [7], and the 2025 modified coronal series of 40 patients [9]. A 2009 series reported 30 endoscopic lifts with cortical tunnel fixation [10].
